extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent practitioners and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether patent claims are directed to patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101 using a two-step analysis: (1) whether the claim is directed to a statutory category and (2) whether it is wholly directed to a judicial exception. Primarily written for patent examiners but also used by applicants and practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step subject matter eligibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two criteria for determining subject matter eligibility and both must be satisfied. The claimed invention (1) must be directed to one of the four statutory categories, and (2) must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception. The following two step analysis is used to evaluate these criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Step 1: determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter). If not, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101. Even if Step 1 fails, Step 2 should still be conducted when an amendment might cure the defect. Apply Step 2: determine whether the claim wholly embraces a judicial exception (laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas) or instead is a particular practical application of an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process (statutory category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Process – an act, or a series of acts or steps. (Cites: Gottschalk v. Benson; NTP v. Research in Motion; 35 U.S.C. 100(b); Bilski v. Kappos.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process is a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result; must be limited to a particular practical application to be statutory (see later factors regarding machine-or-transformation and practical application). Not every claimed method qualifies as a statutory process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine (statutory category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine – a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices. Includes mechanical devices or combinations of devices to perform functions and produce effects or results. (Cites: Burr v. Duryee; Corning v. Burden.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For product/machine claims, tangible structural elements that evidence a particular practical application favor eligibility. Claims that recite a machine but include no tangible structural elements under BRI may be construed to embrace the underlying concept and be ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture (statutory category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacture – an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving to these materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations, whether by handlabor or by machinery. (Cites: Diamond v. Chakrabarty.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacture claims are typically tangible and their claim limitations often make practical application self-evident; evaluate whether claimed limitations are tangible and limit the claim to a particular application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of matter (statutory category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition of matter – all compositions of two or more substances and all composite articles, whether result of chemical union or mechanical mixture, or gases, fluids, powders or solids. (Cites: Chakrabarty.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition claims are product-oriented and eligibility often follows if the claim does not recite a judicial exception or if any recited exception is practically applied in the tangible composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of non-statutory subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to one of the statutory categories: transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., a propagating electrical or electromagnetic signal per se), a naturally occurring organism, a human per se, a legal contractual agreement, a game defined as a set of rules, a computer program per se, a company, and a mere arrangement of printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these examples when assessing whether a claim is within the four categories. If the broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification encompasses such non-statutory embodiments, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth across statutory and non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (under the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim when read in light of the specification and in view of one skilled in the art) embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim language, when broadly read, includes non-statutory embodiments (e.g., a computer-readable medium that can be a carrier wave), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is appropriate. Consider whether amendment could restrict the claim to statutory embodiments; still perform Step 2 if amendment might cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions and 'practical application' concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicially recognized exceptions include laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas. While these exceptions are not patentable, methods and products employing them to perform a real-world function may be eligible if the claim as a whole is a particular practical application of the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the claim as a whole to determine whether it is merely the exception itself (ineligible) or a particular practical application (eligible). Practical application relates to how the exception is applied in a real-world product or process, not merely to the result. Practical application evidence can show the subject matter is not abstract and does not preempt substantially all uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application for product claims (machines/manufactures/compositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed product falls within one of the product categories and does not recite judicially excepted subject matter, it qualifies. If a judicial exception is recited, determine if it has been practically applied in the product. Eligible products are non-naturally occurring, tangible embodiments formed of elements/parts that embody a specific, tangible practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangible structural claim limitations provide evidence of a practical application (e.g., a cup as application of containing liquid; magnetic door latch as application of magnetism). Claims that recite a product but lack tangible limitations under the broadest reasonable interpretation may be viewed as embracing the abstract concept and be ineligible. Evaluate whether the claimed structure limits the claim so it does not cover substantially all practical uses of the underlying concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption / coverage of substantially all practical applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a practical application has been established, the limited occurrence of preemption must be evaluated to determine whether the claim impermissibly covers substantially all practical applications of the judicially excepted subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim covers substantially all practical applications of the exception, it is not patent-eligible; if it covers only a particular practical application, it may be eligible. Assess claim scope carefully in view of the specification and possible embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application for process claims and machine-or-transformation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim must be limited to a particular practical application to be statutory. The machine-or-transformation test remains a useful investigative tool: a claimed process is surely patent-eligible if (1) it is tied to a particular machine or apparatus, or (2) it transforms a particular article into a different state or thing. The test is not sole determinant but provides important factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every method is statutory; consider whether recited structure or a transformative component meaningfully limits the claim. Field-of-use limitations and mere post-solution activity generally do not make an abstract idea patentable (Flook). Use the listed factors (below) to weigh evidence for or against abstractness; consider multiple factors together rather than relying on one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor: whether the method involves or is executed by a particular machine or apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the method involves or is executed by a particular machine or apparatus; the machine-or-transformation test is a useful investigative tool for determining whether some claimed inventions are processes under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant subfactors: (a) the particularity or generality of the machine elements (specific identification of the machine weighs toward eligibility); (b) whether the machine implements the steps of the method (integral use weighs toward eligibility; mere object on which method operates weighs against); (c) whether the machine's involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use (nominal contribution or mere data-gathering/field-of-use weighs against). For computer-implemented processes, programming that causes a general purpose computer to perform the claimed steps may be sufficient to render it a particular machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented processes: programming and 'computer-aided' limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer implemented processes, a general purpose computer may be sufficiently particular when programmed to perform the process steps; such programming creates a new machine because a general purpose computer becomes a special purpose computer once programmed. However, adding a 'computer-aided' limitation without explaining how the computer aids the method is insufficient to render an abstract concept eligible (DealerTrack v. Huber).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must clearly convey that the computer is programmed to perform the steps (i.e., describe how/extent/significance of computer involvement). Mere recitation of a computer or the Internet, or generic 'computer-aided' language, can be insufficient if the claim is otherwise abstract and would preempt substantially all practical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use and 'insignificant extra-solution activity' are not meaningful limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'field-of-use' limitation does not impose actual boundaries on the scope of the claimed invention. Insignificant 'extra-solution' activity means activity that is not central to the purpose of the method invented by the applicant (e.g., gathering data when all applications of the method would require data gathering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on mere field-of-use or token extra steps to render an abstract idea patentable. Such limitations are often insufficient to overcome a §101 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors are illustrative, not exclusive — weigh all relevant factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The listed factors are intended as useful examples and are not exclusive or limiting. New factors may be developed especially for emerging technologies, and examiners should modify factors to take into account developments in precedential case law and prosecution issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh relevant factors both for and against patent-eligibility; consider that only some factors may be present. Do not conclude solely based on a single factor while ignoring others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to a §101 rejection — amendments and persuasive arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper response to a rejection based on failure to claim patent-eligible subject matter would be an amendment adding additional steps/features or amending existing steps/features that integrate the natural principle into the process (by practically applying or making use of the principle) and are sufficient to limit the application of the natural principle to more than the principle itself + steps that do more than simply 'apply it' at a high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amend by adding meaningful limitations that confine the use to particular applications; present persuasive arguments that additional steps add 'something significantly more' than merely describing the natural principle. Showing that steps are not routine, well-known, or conventional can help. Examples: constructing a sanitizing device that integrates UV light rather than merely exposing to sunlight; adding nonconventional testing or treatment steps beyond routine blood sampling when claiming a blood glucose–disease correlation.
